statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: British Columbia Corporate Registry (bcregistry.ca) – Name Reservation Online
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: A proposed corporate name must be distinctive and not confusing with existing business names, trademarks, or reserved names in British Columbia. The name may be in English or French; if a foreign language or non-Roman script is used, a transliteration into English or French must be provided for Registrar review. The legal element for an unlimited liability company must be 'Unlimited Liability Company' or the abbreviation 'ULC' (or equivalent in English/French) included. The Registrar applies section 24 of the BC Business Corporations Act and the Name Regulations.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the name reservation is rejected, the incorporator may file a Request for Reconsideration with the Registrar of Companies through bcregistry.ca within 30 days after the rejection notice, stating the grounds and submitting additional evidence of distinctiveness, consent letters, or disclaimers. The Registrar will issue a written determination. If the determination remains adverse, the applicant may seek judicial review before the Supreme Court of British Columbia under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c 241, naming the Registrar as respondent. To avoid delay, an alternative name reservation may be filed concurrently, and the original incorporation can proceed under a due diligence The name reservation validity is 56 days, renewable once.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: For a ULC manufacturing dental clear aligner sheets, a virtual office is accepted solely for the statutory registered office and records office address provided a physical street address in British Columbia and a registered agent are maintained. The actual manufacturing facility must be a physical location; virtual-only operations do not comply with Health Canada Medical Devices Regulations for a thermoforming and trimming facility. The BC Business Corporations Act requires a registered office open to public inspection; a maildrop without a street address and document acceptance service is not sufficient.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low (approximately 5% per annum) for BC Registrar inspections of the registered office; however, Health Canada Medical Devices Directorate may conduct unannounced quality-system inspections at the manufacturing site, increasing overall on-site inspection risk to approximately 15% per annum.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for the Business Number (BN), corporate income tax, and GST/HST; registration is generally initiated through CRA Business Registration Online or My Business Account. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) administers customs registration and the CARM Client Portal. The British Columbia Ministry of Finance administers provincial sales tax through eTaxBC.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: The British Columbia unlimited liability corporation must obtain a nine-digit CRA Business Number and register applicable CRA program accounts, including RT for GST/HST, RC for corporation income tax, RP for payroll, and RM for import-export activities. A foreign-owned corporation may register through CRA Business Registration Online where eligible, by telephone, or by submitting Form RC1 and supporting incorporation, director, ownership, registered-office, and authorized-representative information. The corporation should register for a GST/HST account before making taxable supplies when the small-supplier threshold is exceeded or voluntary registration is elected. It should register for a CBSA importer-exporter RM account through CARM before commercial importing or exporting. A BC PST account through eTaxBC is required where the corporation makes taxable retail sales, leases, or provides taxable software or services in British Columbia. CRA and provincial registration does not itself establish Canadian tax residence; residence, permanent establishment, management, and treaty facts remain separately determinative.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: A British Columbia ULC is a corporation and is generally subject to Canadian corporate income tax at the entity level; Canada has no general domestic check-the-box election that converts a corporation into a partnership or disregarded entity. An eligible ULC may potentially make a United States federal entity-classification election on IRS Form 8832 if the relevant US eligibility requirements are met. That US election does not change the Canadian legal form or automatically change Canadian tax treatment. Cross-border payments, foreign tax credits, treaty entitlement, hybrid-entity treatment, and mismatch outcomes must be reviewed under the Canada-US treaty, Canadian anti-hybrid rules, and the applicable foreign tax law. A corporation may also make specific Canadian elections, such as capital-cost allowance, fiscal-period, GST/HST reporting-period, and other statutory elections, but these are not pass-through elections.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) at the federal level, with British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST) applying separately to specified taxable goods and services. British Columbia does not impose a harmonized sales tax.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: GST registration is generally mandatory when taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 in a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters, subject to the detailed small-supplier rules. Voluntary registration is permitted in many cases below the threshold. British Columbia PST has separate registration rules and generally no equivalent universal CAD 30,000 threshold; registration depends on the nature and location of taxable retail sales, leases, and taxable services. The standard BC PST rate is generally 7%, subject to statutory exemptions and product-specific rules.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada and British Columbia do not generally require real-time electronic invoice clearance, government pre-approval, or digital fiscal stamping for ordinary domestic B2B supplies. GST/HST registrants must issue compliant invoices or receipts on request, maintain electronic or paper records, preserve transaction-level tax evidence, and report GST/HST using the assigned filing period. Electronic records must remain accessible and reliable for CRA audit purposes. CRA electronic filing and payment obligations may apply based on registrant status and filing requirements. Customs declarations are submitted electronically through CBSA systems, including CARM and the Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS), where applicable; this customs reporting is not a domestic e-invoice clearance regime.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: For GST purposes, goods exported from Canada may generally be zero-rated where the statutory export conditions are satisfied and the supplier retains evidence that the goods were shipped or delivered outside Canada. Certain orthodontic appliances and related dental appliances may also qualify for GST zero-rating under the medical-device provisions when the statutory product, purchaser, prescription, or supply conditions are met; classification must be confirmed for the precise clear-aligner product and transaction chain. Domestic manufacturing inputs and services are generally acquired with GST, and a GST registrant may recover eligible GST through input tax credits when the inputs are used in commercial activities. Offshore services may be zero-rated only where the relevant place-of-supply and non-resident-use conditions are met; services physically performed in Canada, services related to Canadian real property, and services used in Canada may remain taxable. BC PST generally does not apply to goods exported for use outside British Columbia when the statutory exemption conditions and documentary evidence are satisfied, but manufacturing, resale, and medical-device exemptions must be analyzed separately.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canadian Export Declaration through CERS where export reporting is required; exports to the United States are generally subject to different reporting treatment unless an exception or controlled-goods rule applies
Commercial invoice identifying the exporter, consignee, buyer, description, quantity, value, currency, tariff classification, origin, and delivery terms
Packing list and transport evidence, including bill of lading, air waybill, courier manifest, or equivalent carrier record
Proof of delivery or foreign import documentation, where available, and records demonstrating that the goods left Canada
Export permits, certificates, or controlled-goods documentation where required by the Export and Import Permits Act or other applicable legislation
GST/HST invoices, purchase orders, customer contracts, shipping instructions, and accounting records supporting zero-rated treatment
Inward remittance or payment evidence where commercially available; Canada generally does not impose a universal statutory inward-remittance certificate requirement for GST export zero-rating
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Canada generally has no universal foreign-exchange control regime requiring export proceeds to be repatriated within 180 days. Zero-rating can be denied or clawed back where the supplier cannot prove export, the goods were delivered or used in Canada, the product does not satisfy a medical-device zero-rating provision, or the transaction was misrepresented. The resulting GST, interest, and applicable penalties may be assessed retroactively, subject to statutory limitation periods and relevant statute-extension rules. CRA may impose gross-negligence penalties, failure-to-file or failure-to-remit penalties, false-statement penalties, and record-keeping penalties where the facts support them. GST registrants may be denied input tax credits where invoices, importer records, payment evidence, or commercial-use documentation are insufficient. False customs declarations may result in administrative monetary penalties, seizure, reassessment of duties and taxes, and prosecution under the Customs Act or related legislation. BC PST exemptions may be denied with reassessment of tax, interest, and provincial penalties where resale, export, medical-device, or manufacturing documentation is incomplete or inaccurate.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), Ottawa, Ontario, constituted by the Bank of Canada Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. B-2). The Bank issues Canadian-dollar legal tender, conducts monetary policy, and provides settlement accounts for Payments Canada's Lynx high-value payment system, which replaced the Large Value Transfer System. Canada has no dedicated foreign-exchange control board; residual administration is split among the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for federally chartered financial institutions, the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for anti-money-laundering and cross-border electronic-fund-transfer reporting under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17), and the Minister of Finance under the Investment Canada Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 28, 1st Supp.) for non-resident ownership of Canadian businesses.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada accepted IMF Article VIII obligations effective 15 December 1952 and maintains untrammelled convertibility on both current and capital accounts; there are no prior approvals, quotas, surrender requirements, or documentary FX licensing for profit remittance, foreign-direct investment, or trade settlements. The practical remittance constraint is tax rather than exchange control: distributions by the BC ULC to a US shareholder are dividends under the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1, 5th Supp.), subject to Part XIII non-resident withholding at 25% statutory, reduced to 15% for portfolio shareholders and 5% for a US corporation owning at least 10% of voting shares under Article X of the Canada-US Tax Convention (1980). The ULC is a body corporate for Canadian tax purposes, so the US check-the-box election (IRS Form 8832) does not change Canadian characterization; a current Canadian tax opinion should confirm whether the historical section 216(1) election remains viable for the specific shareholder structure after the 2018 federal-budget restriction. Intercompany loan repayments are fully convertible, subject only to the thin-capitalisation safe harbour of ITA section 18(4) (1.5:1 debt-to-equity for treaty-protected non-residents) and to Part XIII on interest if the loan carries non-arm's-length terms.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory export-proceeds surrender obligation, no mandatory conversion timeline, and no required percentage of foreign-currency receipts to be repatriated or exchanged. The ULC may retain USD in a Canadian Schedule I bank's USD clearing account, in a US correspondent account, or offshore. Mandatory compliance touchpoints: (i) every Canadian financial intermediary must report international electronic fund transfers of CAD 10,000 or more to FINTRAC; the ULC is not the filer but must preserve wire advice records for reconciliation; (ii) export declarations must be filed with the Canada Border Services Agency for shipments exceeding CAD 2,000; (iii) exported thermoplastics aligner sheets are zero-rated for GST/HST under Part V, Schedule VI, Excise Tax Act, requiring shipment documentation, commercial invoices, and proof of export; (iv) Export Development Canada (EDC) accounts-receivable insurance is available without exchange-control consequence; (v) annual Form T106 is required for non-arm's-length transactions with the US parent if the aggregate exceeds CAD 1 million.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Medium as an auxiliary collection and settlement overlay; Low as a primary treasury relationship. Canada has no EU-style EMI licence; the governing regime is the Retail Payment Activities Act (S.C. 2021, c. 23, in force November 2024), which requires payment service providers, including Stripe, Wise, Payoneer, and Airwallex, to register with the Bank of Canada, safeguard end-user funds, and comply with operational-risk standards. Legal constraints: fintech wallet balances are not demand deposits and are not CDIC-insured; PSP accounts cannot issue commercial letters of credit, grant revolving credit, or serve as the remittance account for CRA payroll source deductions; PSPs generally require a Schedule I bank confirmation for high-risk or unlimited-liability entities and will not onboard a BC ULC with 100% non-resident UBOs without a resolution from the ULC's board. Recommended treasury architecture: use a Schedule I bank as the root clearing account for all payable and payroll activities; connect Stripe to the ULC's CAD operating account via Repetitive Account Credit for platform card settlements; use a Wise Business multi-currency wallet only as a collection node for EU and UK dental-distributor payments, with daily sweeping of balances back to the Schedule I root account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote onboarding is legally permissible under FINTRAC's flexible identification guidance, which permits verification without physical presence using dual-source documentary checks or a verification agent. In commercial practice for a BC ULC with a 100% US shareholder and non-resident directors, the bank will require: (i) an in-person onboarding interview with at least one Canadian-resident director or senior officer at the bank's business banking centre in Vancouver, presenting original photo identification; (ii) notarized signatures of any US directors on account-opening resolutions, with couriered original corporate documents; (iii) video-conference confirmation with the relationship manager as a supplement, not as a substitute; (iv) certified copies of the BC Registry Services (Corporate Online) extract, Articles of Incorporation, Notice of Articles, Unanimous Shareholder Agreement if any, and CRS/FATCA self-certification forms including Form RC518; and (v) an actual completion timeline of two to six weeks. For a capital escrow sub-account opened simultaneously with incorporation, banks may allow a conditional account pre-funding pending final compliance sign-off.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident US parent owning 100% of an unlimited liability company whose corporate name does not indicate unlimited liability, creating a classification mismatch for the bank's legal-entity risk engine.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified Notice of Articles and Certificate of Incorporation from BC Registry Services; current share-capital register showing the US parent as the sole registered and beneficial owner; IRS Form 8832 check-the-box election confirming US tax transparency; FINTRAC-compliant beneficial-ownership declaration identifying the US parent at the 25% ownership/control threshold; BC legal opinion confirming the ULC is a body corporate with capacity to open bank accounts and bind itself; and a board resolution appointing the banking signatories.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Capital injection of USD 200,000 to USD 500,000 arriving through a money-services business (Wise or similar) rather than a direct bank wire, triggering enhanced source-of-funds scrutiny.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed share-subscription and capital-contribution agreement; originating US bank statement from the parent's bank showing the exact funding wire; chain-of-funds memorandum tracing the MSB remitter to the US parent; board resolution approving the capital plan and escrow restriction; current Form T106 or exemption analysis; IRS Form 5471/5472 filing confirmation where applicable; declaration that funds will remain in the Capital Escrow Account pending drawdown.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Scope flagged as medical device, causing sanctions-screening and trade-compliance holds on payments to suppliers of PETG resin and aligner packaging.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Health Canada Medical Device Establishment Licence (MDEL) under the Medical Devices Regulations (SOR/98/282) for regulated aligner products; alternative opinion classifying the sheets as unregulated dental-laboratory raw materials under HS 3920.69 / 3920.90; ISO 13485 certificate; technical specification sheet; sample commercial invoice and Canadian Export Reporting System declaration; US FDA establishment registration if exported to the United States; supplier master file with legal-entity names, jurisdictions, and confirmation of eligibility for standard OFAC screening.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Repeated intercompany payments from the US parent for R&D licensing and shared services, creating a thin-capitalisation or Part XIII withholding indicator on the operational account.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed technology-licence and technical-services agreements with arm's-length pricing supported by a transfer-pricing memorandum; detailed withholding-tax remittance schedule showing Part XIII amounts withheld and paid to the CRA; debt-to-equity computation demonstrating compliance with the 1.5:1 safe harbour; annual T106 and T634 filing confirmations; external auditor's letter confirming the ULC's allocated Canadian capital.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: All share-capital injections must flow by SWIFT MT103 from the US parent's bank account in the United States directly to the ULC's USD sub-account at the Canadian bank's US correspondent, using the Canadian bank's ABA routing; the field 70 narrative must read 'INVESTMENT / CA_ULC-SHARE SUBSCRIPTION / AGREEMENT DTD YYYY-MM-DD' with a pre-assigned virtual account number in field 59. Canada has no purpose-code regime, but the bank's cash-management platform requires selection of a purpose category: 'Equity Injection' must be selected instead of 'Goods Trade'. For intercompany loan capital, the narrative must state 'INTERCOMPANY LOAN / TR. 12345', and the bank will require the executed loan agreement plus the transfer-pricing memorandum. Any injection exceeding CAD 10,000 is reported by the bank to FINTRAC. Post-settlement steps: update the securities register within 15 days; file Form T106 if aggregate reportable transactions with the US parent exceed CAD 1 million; the US parent must satisfy IRS Form 5471/5472 and FBAR/Form 8938 reporting. Do not route initial capital through third-party fintech wallets, because MSB-origin wires attract enhanced source-of-funds review and can delay availability by five to ten business days.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Operational supplier payments below CAD 250,000 per invoice: SWIFT MT103 from the USD clearing account through the US correspondent, citing invoice number and Incoterms in field 70; FINTRAC files the EFT report for transactions over CAD 10,000. Large capital-equipment purchases above CAD 250,000: irrevocable sight letter of credit under UCP600 (ICC Uniform Customs and Practice), with required documentation consisting of commercial invoice, clean on-board bill of lading, packing list, certificate of origin, and inspection certificate; a 90-day usance draft may be supported by an EDC guarantee. Intra-group royalty and R&D fees: MT103 with citation of the licence agreement and proof of Part XIII withholding remitted to the CRA. Platform receipts from Stripe and card rails: settled via Repetitive Account Credit into the ULC's CAD operating account on T+2; the treasury desk maintains a minimum CAD balance for payroll and CRA remittances and sweeps surplus to USD to match USD payables. Restricted-currency suppliers (CNY, INR, BRL, TRY): settle in USD to the supplier's offshore correspondent account rather than converting CAD locally; overlay NDFs where the commercial invoice is denominated in the restricted currency but settlement is in USD. Clearing infrastructure: Fedwire and CHIPS on the US leg, Lynx on the CAD leg, and SWIFT for all cross-border messaging; MT202 is used only for interbank cover, never for customer trade payments.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable CAD/USD plain-vanilla FX forwards up to 24 months, documented under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a Canadian Credit Support Annex or the bank's short-form forward-hedge agreement, subject to collateral or credit-line support.
FX swaps (benchmark rollovers) for cash-flow timing on known receivable and payable mismatches between CAD operating inflows and USD trade payables.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for restricted and convex currencies such as CNY, INR, BRL, TRY, KRW, and TWD when a commercial contract is denominated in those currencies but settled in USD; NDFs are not used for the CAD/USD base pair because the Canadian dollar is fully deliverable.

Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CCIRS) converting optional USD-denominated intercompany debt from floating SOFR exposure into fixed CAD or fixed USD, permitted under corporate capacity and subject to bank credit limits and collateral support.

OTC FX options, including European-style forwards with optionality and zero-premium collars, permissible when executed solely to hedge firm contract exposures and approved by the board treasury policy; speculative use is expressly prohibited under the ULC's corporate capacity.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: BC Annual Report under the Business Corporations Act (BCA)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, Province of British Columbia (filed via BC Corporate Online)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within two calendar months after each anniversary of incorporation or amalgamation; anniversary-based recurring annual obligation.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No late-filing monetary penalty is assessed on the annual report, but the Registrar will not issue a certificate of compliance while any annual report is outstanding. Failure to file for two consecutive years permits administrative strike-off and dissolution; post-dissolution directors remain exposed to declared and undisclosed liabilities.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal and British Columbia corporate income tax portions)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency; BC corporate income tax is administered under the Canada-BC Tax Collection Agreement
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within six calendar months after the end of each taxation year; the ULC's taxation year generally follows its fiscal year and cannot exceed 12 months.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing triggers a penalty under Income Tax Act s.162 of 5% of the balance owing plus 1% per full month of delinquency, capped at 12 additional months; CRA may issue demand letters, file legal collection action, and assess director liability for unremitted amounts. Non-filing of the T2 does not itself trigger BC administrative strike-off.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual GST return (where the ULC is a registered GST filer using the annual reporting method)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due no later than three months after the end of the reporting period (fiscal year) for annual filers.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing/remittance penalties under the Excise Tax Act apply (percentage-based monthly penalties together with statutory interest); persistent failure to file can lead to CRA collection enforcement and revocation of GST registration, but not corporate strike-off.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: British Columbia Employer Health Tax annual return (applicable only if annual BC remuneration exceeds CAD 500,000)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Government of British Columbia, Ministry of Finance (eTaxBC)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due annually on or before March 31 following the calendar year in which remuneration was paid.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: BC EHT imposes late-filing and late-payment penalties of 2% of the amount owing for a first one-month default plus 0.5% per additional month, increased to 4% for repeated non-filing; interest accrues from the statutory due date. Non-filing is not a corporate registration strike-off event.
